data: Nationalism and National Identity in the Contemporary World

Belying predictions and expectations around the beginning of the third millennium CE of the inexorable forward march of ‘globalization’ and the advent of a post-national age, passionate expressions of nationalist identity and pride animate and indeed dominate the politics of countries around the world. This is especially true of what Charles Tilly called ‘state-led nationalism’ and Benedict Anderson termed ‘official nationalism.’ Contemporary examples include the White, Christian brand of American nationalism championed by Donald Trump in the United States, the massive growth of English nationalism in Britain, the ascendancy of Hindu nationalism in India, and the rise to prominence and power of messianic forms of Zionism in Israel.
This course focuses on and explains the transition of these forms of nationalism from a deceptive marginality to the political centre-stage, and the transformation in their status from oppositional to mainstream and in some cases official ideologies of nation-statehood. The first part of the course covers the major theoretical perspectives on, approaches to the study of, and debates about nationalism and national identity. The second part is devoted to making sense of, and comparing, a selection of contemporary cases from different world regions. Nations and Nationalism: A Reader (Philip Spencer and Howard Wollman, eds, Edinburgh University Press, 2005) will be a key course text. The other major readings for each week are specified below. The course will be offered in the third trimester of AY 2025-26.
